interfaceCtat.descricao: Interface FIXA do tutor (a mesma tela para todos os problemas): enunciado; DUAS retas numéricas de 0 a 1, uma para cada quantidade (rotuladas "Amount Heather has eaten" e "Amount Dave has eaten"); para cada reta há um campo onde o aluno digita em quantas partes iguais dividi-la (com confirmação) e, depois, marca o ponto da fração correspondente; abaixo, um seletor em que o aluno escolhe UMA destas alternativas: "Heather has eaten less of her pie."; "Dave has eaten less of his pie."; "Both have eaten the same amount of their pies."; botão Hint; botão Done. Os passos do aluno são ações NESSES componentes (dividir cada reta, marcar cada ponto, escolher a alternativa, concluir).

componentes.papel: campo numérico do denominador da primeira reta (em quantas partes dividir) + confirmar
primeira reta numérica; o aluno marca o ponto da primeira fração
campo numérico do denominador da segunda reta + confirmar
segunda reta numérica; o aluno marca o ponto da segunda fração
seletor com as alternativas de comparação; o aluno escolhe uma delas

dicas.texto: What does the denominator tell you about the whole pie?
Represent the eaten pieces and compare them with all the equal pieces in the whole pie.
Heather ate 3 pieces, while the whole pie contains 4 equal pieces.
Select the state showing some, but not all, of the pie eaten, and submit the label for an amount less than one whole.
Which number in a fraction tells how many equal parts make the whole?
Read the denominator and enter that number in the field for the first number line.
In 3/4, look at the number below the fraction bar.
Type the denominator of 3/4 into denom1 and confirm the division.
The numerator tells how many equal parts to count from zero.
Count the equal intervals from 0 toward 1 using the denominator-based divisions.
Heather's amount is three intervals out of the four intervals between 0 and 1.
Starting at zero, count three intervals and click that location on numline1.
Which part of a fraction tells how many equal pieces form the whole?
Read the denominator in Dave's fraction and enter it in the second number-line field.
Dave's fraction is 6/8, and the number below the fraction bar is 8.
Type Dave's denominator into denom2 and confirm the division into equal parts.
The numerator tells how many equal intervals represent the amount eaten.
Start at zero and count the intervals using the eight-part division.
Dave's point is six intervals from zero on a line divided into eight equal intervals.
Starting at zero, count six intervals and click that location on numline2.
Equivalent fractions name the same amount even when their denominators differ.
Compare where both marked points land on their number lines from 0 to 1.
Heather's point is three of four intervals, and Dave's point is six of eight intervals.
Align or inspect the two marked positions and submit the state showing that they coincide.
Use the marked positions rather than comparing the numerators alone.
Read the relationship between the two points and match it to one of the selector statements.
The two points occupy the same position on the 0-to-1 scale.
Choose the statement that says the two people ate the same amount of their pies.
Before finishing, make sure both fractions were represented and compared.
Check the two denominator fields, the two marked points, and the selected comparison.
Heather's line should use 4 parts, Dave's line should use 8 parts, and both points should be marked.
When every component is complete, press the Done button to submit the comparison.

exercicio.statement:
Heather and Dave each received a small pie to enjoy. Heather likes to cut her pie into 4 pieces, and Dave likes to cut his pie into 8 pieces. After enjoying their snack, Heather and Dave compared their pie to see who has eaten less.
Heather has eaten 3/4 of her pie.
Dave has eaten 6/8 of his pie.
Who has eaten less of their pie?
